specification.title: To what extent was the League of Nations a success?

request.prompt: Explain two reasons why the League of Nations struggled to stop aggression in the 1930s. For each, connect the weakness to its practical effect.
request.criterion: Award up to four marks for each of two distinct reasons: identification, accurate supporting detail, explanation of its practical effect and a developed connection to failure to deter aggression. Accept lack of its own army, absence of major powers, limited sanctions, decision-making delays or members prioritising national interests. Do not duplicate reasons. This original eight-mark allocation is not an exam-board mark scheme.
request.explanation: Original evaluation material. Independent content review and reference marking are required before live use. Award only supported rubric points; accept equivalent meaning.
request.answer: The League had no army of its own, so enforcing decisions depended on members providing forces. Governments reluctant to risk war could refuse, leaving threats without credible military backing and reducing deterrence. The USA never joined, leaving an important economy outside sanctions. Aggressors could seek trade outside the League, reducing economic pressure and making sanctions less likely to force withdrawal.
